claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a pre-existing thin native oxide film.
At room temperature, the native oxide film acts as a protective barrier in a harsh chloride-containing environment.
At elevated temperature, thermal effects destabilize the native oxide film.
At elevated temperature, destabilization of the native oxide accelerates localized corrosion relative to an oxide-stripped surface.
The proposed intervention compares Q235 specimens retaining the native oxide with specimens from which it has been removed.
The controlled exposures are conducted at approximately 25°C and 80°C, at 95% relative humidity and fixed chloride concentration.
The integrity and stability of the native oxide film are the proposed structural mediator.
At room temperature, the native oxide remains stable and impedes corrosive chemical reactions.
Elevated temperature produces thermal stresses that compromise the integrity of the native oxide film.
Breakdown of the native oxide film accelerates localized corrosion.
At approximately 25°C, intact-native-oxide specimens will have lower corrosion rates than oxide-stripped specimens.
At approximately 80°C, intact-native-oxide specimens will have higher localized corrosion rates than oxide-stripped specimens.
The proposed comparison uses identical exposure durations for intact-oxide and oxide-stripped specimens.
Corrosion current density, EIS barrier properties, pitting morphology, surface composition, and oxide-film status are proposed as measurable responses.
The proposed mechanism is limited to as-received Q235 steel with its native oxide under the specified chloride, humidity, and temperature conditions.
The results may not extrapolate to engineered passivation layers or substantially different environmental conditions.
